gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 300's 4,800 W is a resistive-only Power Lifting mode in which output stays at 2,400 W (StorageReview), so it is not comparable with the 7,200 W surge of the 3,600 W units, and none puts the makers' cycle ratings on one 80% line.
standout_why: Compared against powerstations.reviews/jackery-3000, both wattpowerstation.com pages, power-verdict.com, thepowerstationreport.com, thesolarlab.com, lightsonlabs.com and powersized.com/reviews. powerstations.reviews lists cycles with their 70% or 80% lines but does not adjust them, and prints the Elite 300 as '2,400 (4,800)' in its continuous (surge) column. Lights On Labs says Jackery's 70% rating 'can't be compared directly' and stops there. wattpowerstation tabulates tested usable Wh but has no Elite 300 row. None mentions lifting, X-Boost or SurgePad modes, and none gives price per rated cycle. So rivals hold the raw cycle and surge numbers (part of it); the lifting-versus-surge correction, a measured usable figure for the Elite 300 and the cost-per-cycle arithmetic are new.
decides: It confirms ChatGPT's split and sharpens it. The Jackery HomePower 3000 stays the pick for motor loads or several appliances at once (3,600 W, 7,200 W surge). The Elite 300 is the value pick only for loads sized against 2,400 W, motors included; on that term it has the longest rating on the 80% line (6,000+ against 3,500 to 4,000) and costs about 18 cents per rated cycle against the Pecron F3000LFP's 26 cents, although the Pecron is $200 cheaper to buy. The Pecron's surge is 4,500 W for 5 s, the lowest of the 3,600 W units, and its tested usable share is the lowest (83%). Outside the angle but it affects the pick: BLUETTI's store now says Elite 300 orders placed on or after Nov 27 ship from Dec 28, which is 31 days and past the four-week rule (the desk note said Dec 14), so compare its Amazon listing before making it a pick. The Pecron is a mid-December pre-order, and Anker's store shows the F3000 sold out with 3 to 7 week shipping.

findings.label: What the 4,800 W figure is
findings.value: Power Lifting mode, not surge: off by default, for pure resistive loads rated 2,400 to 4,800 W only; actual output stays at 2,400 W
findings.note: StorageReview: it 'does not turn the Elite 300 into a full 4,800W power source'; motor and compressor loads should be sized against the normal 2,400 W limit. Its own spec table still labels 4,800 W 'Surge Power', and powerstations.reviews prints 2,400 (4,800) in its surge column.

findings.label: Maker's page wording for output and cycles
findings.value: 2,400 W output '(4,800 W lifting)'; no separate surge figure; 'Battery Cycle Life 6000+' with no capacity threshold; 10 ms switchover
findings.note: The page states 3,014 Wh (3,014.4 Wh in its FAQ). It shows only 'Global Warranty' badges, with no warranty length in years.

findings.label: Cycle life on the 80% line
findings.value: More than 6,000 cycles to 80% of original capacity
findings.note: StorageReview reporting BLUETTI's rating; BLUETTI's product page gives the count without the threshold. Arithmetic: 6,000 / 365 = 16.4 years of one full cycle a day. StorageReview also gives a 5-year warranty and 57.98 lb.

findings.label: Measured usable AC output
findings.value: 2.67 kWh out, about 88.6% of the rated 3,014.4 Wh; 3.49 kWh drawn from the wall for a 0 to 100% charge
findings.note: Arithmetic: 2,670 / 3,014.4 = 88.6%; wall-to-outlet round trip 2.67 / 3.49 = 76.5%. At $1,099 that is $0.41 per usable Wh. Different tester and method from wattpowerstation's figures, so treat the comparison as approximate. StorageReview measured 8 ms switchover to battery and 8.25 ms back.

findings.label: Store price and ship date
findings.value: $1,099.00 (compare-at $1,199.00); orders placed on or after Nov 27 ship starting Dec 28
findings.note: Price from storecheck.py and the page; ship notice from the page. Nov 27 to Dec 28 is 31 days. Arithmetic: $1,099 / 6,000 cycles = 18.3 cents per rated cycle; $1,099 / (3.0144 kWh x 6,000) = 6.1 cents per rated lifetime kWh, ignoring fade.

findings.label: Surge, cycles, price and ship date
findings.value: 3,600 W continuous, surge 4,500 W for 5 s (1.25x); 3,500+ cycles to 80%; $899.00, pre-order, ships mid-December
findings.source_title: PECRON F3000LFP Portable Power Station 3600W 3072Wh PRE-ORDER | Ships Mid Dec
findings.note: Read through storecheck.py search on pecron.com (listing title and description; the full page returned 429). Also: 1,800 W AC charging '2 hours', 15 A max; '2+3 years warranty'. Arithmetic: $899 / 3,500 = 25.7 cents per rated cycle; $899 / (3.072 kWh x 3,500) = 8.4 cents per rated lifetime kWh; 3,500 / 365 = 9.6 years of daily cycles.

findings.label: Where the 3,600 W comes out, surge and SurgePad
findings.value: 3,600 W total; each NEMA 5-20R outlet 2,400 W max (20 A); the full 3,600 W from one socket only at the TT-30R (30 A); 7,200 W surge; 4,860 W SurgePad
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3000 Portable Power Station
findings.note: Anker lists 4,860 W SurgePad separately from the 7,200 W surge. AC charging 1,800 W max on the 120 V 15 A cable; 3,600 W only through TT-30 or the EV adapter. 20 ms switchover, 91.5 lb.

findings.label: Cycle rating and availability at Anker's store
findings.value: 4,000 cycles, no capacity threshold on the page; listed sold out, 'all F3000 orders will ship within 3–7 weeks'
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3000 Portable Power Station
findings.note: The price did not load ('Price Loading'). powerstations.reviews lists the rating as 4,000 to 80%; Anker's own page does not say.

findings.label: Surge versus X-Boost, cycle wording, price
findings.value: 3,600 W continuous, 7,200 W surge; X-Boost 'up to 4600W'; no cycle count, only '10 years of reliable power'; series from $1,369, Ultra Plus $1,599
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Series Portable Power Station (3072Wh)
findings.note: Read through storecheck.py search on us.ecoflow.com (listing text; the full page returned 429). The listing says 'DELTA 3 Ultra: Limited Stock Remaining. No Restock Planned.' 10 ms auto-switch; warranty 3 years plus 2 on app registration. Ultra Plus price is from its own listing, /products/ecoflow-delta-3-ultra-plus-portable-power-station-3072wh.

findings.label: Cycle rating and surge, as two rival pages report them
findings.value: 4,000 cycles to 70% of capacity, a lower bar than the 80% other makers use; 3,600 W continuous, 7,200 W surge (2.0x); 20 ms switchover
findings.source_title: Best portable power stations for home backup (2026) | Lights On Labs
findings.note: powerstations.reviews/jackery-3000 gives the same figures. Jackery's own page and FAQ returned 429 and 403 today, so this is not from the maker. On the 80% line the count is therefore below 4,000; a straight-line reading aid (30 points lost over 4,000 cycles gives 20 points at about 2,670) is an assumption, not a Jackery figure. Lights On Labs also says the 5-year warranty applies only when bought from jackery.com, otherwise 3 years.

findings.label: Tested usable AC capacity for the rivals
findings.value: Jackery HomePower 3000 2,759 Wh (90%); Anker F3000 2,613 Wh (85%); EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Plus 2,611 Wh (85%); Pecron F3000LFP 2,550 Wh (83%)
findings.source_title: Portable Power Station Reviews: Tested Capacity & Prices (Watt Power Station)
findings.note: Watt Power Station's 'middle of each model's counted tests'; one test each except the Anker (two). It has no Elite 300 row. With today's store prices: Pecron $899 / 2,550 = $0.35 per usable Wh; Elite 300 $1,099 / 2,670 = $0.41.

findings.label: What the cited rival does with cycle thresholds and surge
findings.value: Lists cycles with mixed 70% and 80% lines and no adjustment; no lifting or boost modes mentioned; Elite 300 shown as 2,400 (4,800) surge; ALLPOWERS R3500 3,500 cycles with no end-of-life percentage
findings.source_title: Jackery 3000: the 3000 Pro, the HomePower 3000, and which to buy
findings.note: Its only cost metric is price per rated Wh. This is the page ChatGPT cited in both chats.
